questions.q: Why does a general wiki page describing how a pipeline works tend to go stale?
options: General descriptions are always more accurate than specific ones
This only happens to documentation written by inexperienced engineers
Wiki pages are technically incapable of being updated after publishing
It lives somewhere separate from the thing it describes, so nobody remembers to update it when the system changes
questions.explain: This is a structural problem, not laziness — documentation survives only when something forces it to stay current.

questions.q: What makes a runbook different from a general description of a system?
options: It's a specific, step-by-step response to a specific, known alert — exactly what to do right now, not a general overview
Runbooks only apply to Fabric Capacity billing issues
Runbooks are written once and never need updating, unlike general docs
Runbooks are identical to a data contract in structure and purpose
questions.explain: It gets opened during a real incident, so its gaps get noticed and fixed immediately rather than discovered by nobody, ever.

questions.q: Why does a README committed in the same folder as an Eventstream's definition stay more accurate than a wiki page?
options: It gets updated in the same pull request as a change to that Eventstream, since it's sitting right there during code review
READMEs are automatically regenerated by Fabric whenever an Eventstream changes
Wiki pages are always more likely to be reviewed than a README
A README in the same folder has no real advantage over a separate wiki page
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 46's point about item definitions living in Git as readable, reviewable text.

questions.q: Why is Lesson 50's data contract described as "self-enforcing" documentation?
options: Self-enforcing means it updates its own text automatically without human input
It's checked in CI (Lesson 45), so a change contradicting it fails the build rather than just quietly diverging from an unread description
This only applies to contracts, not to any other kind of documentation
Data contracts don't actually require any enforcement mechanism
questions.explain: This is the model worth generalizing wherever possible — documentation that's checked, not just written.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the common thread between a runbook, docs-next-to-code, and a self-enforcing contract?
options: They are all identical documents with different names
None of these actually prevent documentation from going stale
Each survives because something forces it to stay current — being read during an incident, sitting in the same review, or being checked automatically
Only the data contract among the three actually stays accurate over time
questions.explain: This is the structural insight the lesson builds toward: proximity or enforcement, not good intentions, is what keeps documentation accurate.
